title: Second Harmonic Generation Spectroscopy of the Surface Charge Density Wave in the Weyl Semimetal CoSi
authors: Awadhesh K. Das, Wesley E. Deeg, Sujan Subedi, Chandra Shekhar, Claudia Felser, Darius H. Torchinsky
abstract: Using temperature-dependent rotational anisotropy second harmonic generation (RA-SHG), we identify a charge density wave (CDW) instability on the CoSi (001) face with an onset temperature at $90.0 \pm 0.8$ K. The SHG response tracks the order parameter amplitude, dominated by two nonlinear tensor elements, whose background-subtracted intensity evolves with temperature as a power law. The extracted critical exponent $β= 0.30 \pm 0.03$ is consistent with the 3D XY universality class, an unexpected result for a nominally two-dimensional surface layer. No corresponding anomaly is observed in the bulk response, establishing the transition as a purely surface-driven phase transition. We attribute this unexpected scaling to the coupling between surface Fermi-arc states and the bulk topology they are tied to, grounded in a previously observed intra-unit-cell phase relationship between surface sublayers that gives the order parameter intrinsic three-dimensional structure.
summary: Researchers used RA-SHG spectroscopy on the CoSi surface to study a CDW transition at 90 K. They found the transition follows the 3D XY critical scaling, which is unexpected for a 2D surface. This suggests that the CDW order parameter has an intrinsic 3D character due to coupling with the underlying bulk topology of the Weyl semimetal.
main_problem: To determine the nature and dimensionality of a Charge Density Wave (CDW) instability occurring on the surface of a Weyl Semimetal.
main_result: The CDW transition exhibits critical behavior consistent with the 3D XY universality class, despite being confined to a nominally two-dimensional surface layer.
method: Rotational Anisotropy Second Harmonic Generation (RA-SHG) spectroscopy was used to measure the temperature dependence of the surface nonlinear susceptibility tensor elements.
model_or_system: The study investigates the CoSi (001) surface, a Weyl Semimetal, where the CDW order parameter is probed. The analysis compares the observed critical exponent to theoretical predictions for phase transitions.
key_observables: Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) intensity, which tracks the CDW order parameter amplitude; the critical exponent $\beta$; and the transition temperature $T_{CDW}$.
important_parameters: Critical exponent $\beta = 0.30 \pm 0.03$; Transition temperature $T_{CDW} = 90.0 \pm 0.8$ K; Comparison to 3D XY universality class.
main_assumptions: The apparent contradiction between 2D surface confinement and 3D XY scaling is resolved by assuming the CDW order parameter possesses an intrinsic three-dimensional structure due to coupling between surface sublayers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the raw RA-SHG data showing anisotropy changes across the transition, and plots detail the temperature dependence of background-subtracted SHG intensity and ratios of tensor elements.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the experimental setup and the CDW transition using RA-SHG. It then analyzes the temperature scaling of the SHG signal to extract the critical exponent, concluding that the 3D XY class applies due to underlying 3D coupling mechanisms.
why_interesting: The finding of 3D XY critical behavior on a 2D surface challenges simple dimensionality arguments in critical phenomena, suggesting that topological coupling can induce higher-dimensional phase coherence.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic diagram of the experimental setup for SHG measurements. Optics are WGP-wire grid polar- izer, QWP-quarter wave plate, P-polarizer, LF-longpass fil- ter, M-mirror, CM-concave mirror, A-analyzer, L-lens, SF- shortpass filter and PMT-photomultiplier tube. The funda- mental (ω) and second harmonic (2ω) beams are represented in red and blue, respectively. Polar plots (a) I∥and (b) I⊥ show raw data (red) with fits (black) to surface point group C1. Here P and A are co-rotated, i.e., parallel for I∥and perpendicular for I⊥.

Fig. 2. RA-SHG measurements on the CoSi (001) surface showing the evolution of the angular response across the CDW transition. The SHG intensity as a function of input polariza- tion angle ϕ is presented for the (a) fixed horizontal analyzer IH, (b) fixed vertical analyzer IV . Panels (c) and (d) show the corresponding polar plots at 105 K (red, T > TCDW ) and 62 K (blue, T < TCDW ), together with global fits to the sur- face symmetry point group (solid black and orange curves). A pronounced change in the angular anisotropy appears below TCDW , signaling the onset of surface ordering.

Fig. 3. Panels (a), (b), (c), and (d) show the background- subtracted temperature-dependent peak SHG intensity for the IH, IV , I∥, and I⊥geometries, respectively, reconstructed using all six surface tensor elements (Supplementary Fig. 3) and evaluated through the expression in Supplementary Sec- tion S3. The transition temperature TCDW ∼90.0 K from the fit is marked by the black dashed lines. Panels (e) and (f) show the temperature dependence of the two dominant sur- face tensor elements, χ(2) xxy and χ(2) yxx, extracted from global fits along with a line to guide the eye.

Fig. 4. Temperature-dependent SHG response of the bulk CoSi over the temperature interval 60–110 K. The SHG in- tensities for the IH and IV channels are shown in panels (a) and (c). The angular plots in panels (b) and (d) are identi- cal above and below TCDW with global fits to Space Group 198, indicating the absence of temperature-driven modifica- tion on this face. Panel (e) shows the peak SHG intensities for IH, IV , I∥and I⊥, offset by ±0.5 for clarity. No significant temperature-driven transition is observed in the bulk SHG re- sponse.

Fig. 5. Temperature dependence of ratios among the six sur- face tensor elements. The ratio of the two dominant compo- nents, χ(2) xxy/χ(2) yxx (black), remains constant to within a few percent across the entire measured range, including through TCDW , indicating that both components track a common un- derlying quantity. Ratios among the four weak components (χ(2) yyx/χ(2) yyy, χ(2) yyy/χ(2) xxx, χ(2) yyx/χ(2) xxx, and χ(2) xyy/χ(2) yyx) vary only modestly below TCDW but fluctuate more substantially above it.
